16110:
When someone is tolerant, they are willing to allow something to exist or continue — even if they personally dislike it, disagree with it, or find it uncomfortable — without fighting against it, punishing it, or trying to stop it.

A tolerant person sees something that bothers them, and makes a conscious choice: "I'll let this be."
The Single Most Important Thing to Know

Being tolerant does not mean you like or agree with something. It just means you choose not to interfere with it.

This distinction is everything. Tolerance lives in the space between disagreement and hostility. You can hold a firm opinion against something, and still be tolerant of it.
How It's Used in Different Situations

In social life and human relationships — this is the most common use.

A tolerant person accepts that other people have different beliefs, religions, lifestyles, opinions, or habits, and doesn't judge, attack, or try to force change upon them.

  • "She is tolerant of people who hold very different political views."
  • "A tolerant society allows its citizens to live by their own values."
  • "He was tolerant toward people whose lifestyle he didn't personally agree with."

In a physical or medical sense — when a body, a plant, or a system can handle something without being badly affected by it.

  • "She is surprisingly tolerant of spicy food." (It doesn't hurt or bother her.)
  • "His body became tolerant of the drug after several weeks." (It adapted; it no longer reacted strongly.)
  • "This plant species is tolerant of dry, harsh conditions." (It survives and functions despite difficulty.)

In technical or scientific contexts — a system that is tolerant can keep functioning even when something goes wrong or varies from ideal.

  • "The design is fault-tolerant." (It keeps working even if part of it fails.)

These three are easy to mix up. Here's how they differ:

Approving means you actively like it or think it is right.
Accepting means you embrace it as normal or valid.
Tolerant means you allow it to exist, even though you may not like or agree with it.

A parent might say: "I don't approve of my child's decision, but I'll be tolerant of it." This means: "I disagree, but I won't try to stop them or punish them for it."

Tolerance is not warmth. It is not hostility either. It is the conscious, deliberate middle ground.

You only "tolerate" something that is, at least to some degree, difficult for you to accept. The word quietly carries a signal of friction — of something you find uncomfortable, wrong, or disagreeable, yet choose to leave alone.

This means you would never say you "tolerate" something you love or fully enjoy. You enjoy those things. You don't tolerate them.

  • If someone loves loud music, you don't say they "tolerate" it — you say they love it.
  • If someone agrees fully with an opinion, you don't say they "tolerate" it — you say they share it.

So whenever you hear or use the word tolerant, understand that there is a quiet tension underneath it: "This is not what I would choose, but I will allow it."
How Strong or Weak Tolerance Can Be

Tolerance exists on a scale:

  • Barely tolerant — the person is struggling to hold back their frustration or disapproval. They are doing the minimum to not react.
  • Quite tolerant — the person is generally open-minded and relaxed when faced with differences.
  • Extremely tolerant — very little offends, irritates, or disturbs this person. They have a very wide range of things they can peacefully coexist with.

The opposite of tolerant is intolerant.

An intolerant person is unwilling to accept things that are different from their own beliefs, preferences, or way of life. They may react with anger, discrimination, or force.

  • "He was intolerant of any opinion that challenged his own."
  • "Intolerance of other cultures can cause serious conflict in society."

• Tolerate (verb): "I can tolerate the noise, but it isn't easy."
  • Tolerance (noun): "Religious tolerance is essential in a diverse country."
  • Tolerantly (adverb): "She listened tolerantly as he repeated his argument for the third time."
  • Intolerant (adjective — opposite): "He was intolerant of any form of criticism."
  • Intolerance (noun — opposite): "Intolerance leads to division and conflict."

"Tolerant of" is the most natural pairing — you are always tolerant of something or someone.

  • tolerant of differences / criticism / pain / noise
  • tolerant toward others / minorities / newcomers
  • a tolerant society / community / culture
  • a tolerant attitude / approach / person
  • highly / more / less tolerant

Tolerant means: willing to allow something to exist — even when you personally disagree with it, dislike it, or find it difficult — without fighting, punishing, or suppressing it. It is not agreement. It is not love. It is the deliberate, sometimes effortful choice to leave something alone and let it be.
16111:
To tolerate something means to allow it to exist or continue, even though you dislike it, disagree with it, or find it unpleasant. You are not stopping it. You are not fighting it. But you are also not happy about it. You are simply letting it be.

This is the essential tension inside the word: you don't like something, but you put up with it anyway.
The Key Idea That Makes This Word Unique

The most important thing to understand is that "tolerate" always carries a quiet sense of discomfort or disapproval. You never tolerate something you enjoy. You never tolerate something you love. The word only makes sense when there is something negative — some irritation, some disagreement, some pain — and you choose not to act against it.

Think of it this way: tolerating something is like holding something you find unpleasant in your hands and choosing not to throw it away. You don't squeeze it. You don't embrace it. You just... hold it.

This is why the word suggests restraint and patience. To tolerate is to hold yourself back from reacting, even when a part of you wants to.

The word is used in several areas of life.

Tolerating people or their behavior. If your coworker talks loudly on the phone all day and it bothers you, but you say nothing and continue with your work, you are tolerating their behavior. If a parent finds their teenager's messy room frustrating but doesn't argue about it every day, they are tolerating it.

Tolerating situations or conditions. If the temperature in a room is uncomfortably hot but you stay there and don't complain, you are tolerating the heat. A soldier who endures pain without showing it is tolerating that pain. A student who sits through a boring lecture without leaving is tolerating the boredom.

Tolerating beliefs, opinions, or differences. This is a very common and important use of the word. A person who disagrees with someone else's religion, political view, or lifestyle, but allows that person to live freely without interfering — that person is tolerating those differences. This is the meaning behind the concept of tolerance in society: people with different beliefs or backgrounds being allowed to exist alongside each other without being attacked or silenced, even if not everyone agrees with everyone else.

Tolerating a substance (medical or physical use). Your body can also tolerate or fail to tolerate things. If a medicine causes no harmful reaction in your body, your body is tolerating it well. If someone can drink coffee without any problem, their body tolerates caffeine. This use is slightly more neutral — it's about physical capacity rather than a feeling of dislike.

Tolerating something sits on a scale. At the mild end, you might barely notice your discomfort — you're tolerating a slightly squeaky chair. At the strong end, tolerating can mean enduring something deeply unpleasant with great effort — tolerating years of mistreatment at a job, or tolerating severe physical pain.

The common thread is always endurance — you are bearing something, carrying it, without breaking under it or lashing out against it.
How Tolerate Differs from Similar Words

This is where many learners get confused, so pay close attention.

Tolerate vs. Accept. To accept something means you have come to peace with it. You may have once disliked it, but now you are genuinely okay with it. Tolerate does not go that far. You can tolerate something your entire life and never accept it. For example: "She never accepted her son's decision to quit school, but she tolerated it because she didn't want to lose him." She still disapproved — she simply chose not to act on that disapproval.

Tolerate vs. Approve. To approve of something means you think it is good or right. Tolerating something is almost the opposite — you think it is not ideal, but you allow it anyway. You might say: "I don't approve of his habits, but I tolerate them." These two words point in opposite directions.

Tolerate vs. Ignore. To ignore something means you are not paying attention to it, as if it doesn't exist. To tolerate it means you are fully aware of it and its unpleasantness — you just choose not to confront it. Tolerating requires a conscious choice. Ignoring does not.

Tolerate vs. Enjoy. These are total opposites. If you enjoy something, you would never say you are tolerating it. The very presence of "tolerate" signals that enjoyment is absent.

These two negative forms are extremely common and worth understanding on their own.

"Cannot tolerate" means something is so unpleasant that you genuinely cannot bear it — your limit has been reached. "She cannot tolerate the smell of cigarette smoke." "He cannot tolerate injustice." This can describe a physical limit (the smell makes her sick) or an emotional/moral one (injustice deeply upsets him and he refuses to stay silent).

"Will not tolerate" is stronger and more deliberate. It is a firm declaration that you are drawing a line. A teacher might say: "I will not tolerate cheating in this classroom." A parent might say: "I will not tolerate disrespect in this house." This means: this is where my patience ends, and there will be consequences. It carries authority and finality.

Here are a range of examples to help the word come alive:

"She tolerated the pain for as long as she could before asking for medicine." (physical endurance)

"He doesn't agree with his neighbor's choices, but he tolerates them because everyone deserves to live their own life." (social/personal)

"The manager tolerated his employee's constant lateness for months before finally having a conversation about it." (behavioral)

"A free society tolerates many kinds of speech, even speech that some find offensive." (social/political)

"Her body could not tolerate the new medication, so the doctor switched her to a different one." (medical/physical)

"I can tolerate cold weather, but extreme heat is something I really struggle with." (personal capacity)

"He had tolerated years of poor treatment at that company before finally deciding to resign." (endurance over time)

When you see or use the word tolerate, always remember this: there are three things happening at once.

First, there is something unpleasant — a behavior, a condition, a situation, a belief, a substance.

Second, there is a person who is aware of that unpleasantness and does not like it.

Third, that person chooses — sometimes easily, sometimes with great effort — not to stop it, not to fight it, and not to walk away from it.

That entire experience — the dislike, the awareness, and the quiet decision to allow it anyway — is what the word tolerate captures.
16112: "Toll" has three distinct meanings as a noun. Each is common and important to know.
Meaning 1: A fee you pay to use something

A toll is a charge or fee you must pay in order to use a road, bridge, tunnel, or highway. Think of it as "renting" the right to pass through or across something.

For example, some bridges are not free — you pay a small amount of money at a booth, and then you are allowed to cross. That money is called a toll.

"There is a toll of two dollars to use this highway."
"I forgot to bring cash and couldn't pay the toll."

Related words you'll see:

  • Tollbooth — the small booth or gate where you stop and pay
  • Toll road / Tollway — a road where you must pay to drive
  • Toll-free — meaning you don't have to pay (no charge)
Meaning 2: The total cost, damage, or suffering caused by something

This is the most powerful and widely used meaning of the word. Here, a toll refers to the total amount of harm, loss, or suffering that something causes — especially over time or as a result of a bad event.

It answers the question: "How much did this cost in terms of lives, health, money, or well-being?"

The most common example is death toll — the total number of people who died because of a disaster, war, accident, or illness.

"The death toll from the earthquake rose to 500."
"The storm left a devastating toll on the city."

But the damage doesn't have to be physical. A toll can also refer to emotional, mental, or physical strain on a person.

"Years of working long hours took a toll on her health."
"The stress of the job is taking a heavy toll on him."

The phrase "take a toll" (or "take its toll") is extremely common in English. It means that something is slowly causing damage, harm, or exhaustion.

"Lack of sleep takes a toll on your body."
"The constant arguing took a toll on their friendship."

Notice how this meaning is always about cumulative damage — the cost adds up over time, or the final count of something bad.
Meaning 3: The slow, deep ring of a large bell

A toll is also the sound made by a large bell ringing slowly, one strike at a time — the kind you might hear from a church or a clock tower. Each individual ring or strike of the bell is called a toll.

"We heard the toll of the church bell in the distance."
"With each toll of the bell, the crowd grew quieter."

This meaning is less common in everyday speech but appears often in literature and formal writing.

It helps to see that all three meanings share a thread of weight and consequence:

  • You pay something to pass (a fee).
  • Something costs you dearly in harm or suffering (a toll on health/life).
  • A bell marks a solemn moment, slowly and heavily.

In all three, there is a sense of something being counted, charged, or felt deeply.

If you see...It means...
  • "Pay a toll" → You're paying a fee to use a road or bridge.
  • "Death toll" → The total number of deaths from an event.
  • "Take a toll" → Something is causing harm or exhaustion over time.
  • "The toll of the bell" → The slow, deep sound of a large bell ringing.

Master these four uses and you will understand "toll" correctly in virtually every situation you will ever encounter it.
16113: The verb toll has two distinct meanings — one you will encounter often in literature and everyday life, and one that belongs specifically to the world of law. Both are worth knowing.
The Primary Meaning: To Ring a Bell Slowly and Solemnly

When a bell tolls, it does not ring in a fast, cheerful flurry. It rings in slow, heavy, individual strokes — one deep, resonant bong... a pause... then another bong. The sound is deliberate, measured, and serious.

This is the key distinction to hold in your mind: not all bell-ringing is tolling. When church bells ring joyfully for a wedding or a celebration, they peal — bright, rapid, and lively. But when a bell tolls, the ringing is always slow, always grave, always carrying a kind of heaviness in its sound.

What does tolling announce?

Historically and in literature, a bell tolls to signal:

  • A death or a funeral procession
  • A period of communal mourning
  • The time of day, particularly at solemn moments ("The clock tolled midnight.")
  • A grave warning or an event of great importance

How the verb is used grammatically

Toll works in two directions:

The bell itself can be the one tolling. Here, no person needs to be mentioned — the bell just does it on its own, as if it has a voice. For example: "A bell tolled somewhere in the fog." / "The bell tolled three times."

Alternatively, a person can toll the bell — meaning they are the one causing it to ring. For example: "The monk tolled the bell at dawn." / "She tolled the bell once for each of the fallen."

In the first case, the bell is ringing (intransitive — no direct object). In the second, someone is actively ringing the bell (transitive — the bell is the object). Both usages are correct and common.

The emotional weight of "toll"

This is important for a learner: toll is not emotionally neutral. The word almost always lives in the territory of sorrow, loss, solemnity, or the gravity of a significant moment passing. You would never use it to describe a happy sound. The very choice of the word "toll" signals to the reader or listener: something serious is happening here. Writers use it deliberately to set a heavy, mournful tone.

The famous phrase you will almost certainly encounter

There is a line from the poet John Donne that has echoed through centuries of literature, and you will likely meet it:

"Ask not for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee."

Ernest Hemingway later used this as the title of his celebrated novel For Whom the Bell Tolls, bringing the phrase to an even wider audience.

The meaning is worth understanding: In Donne's time, a bell was rung in a town whenever someone died, to let the community know. His point was that when any person dies, that death is not only their loss — because humanity is deeply connected, every death diminishes all of us. So when the bell tolls for a stranger, it is in a sense also tolling for you. The reason this line is so powerful is precisely because of the word "tolls" — that slow, inevitable, heavy ringing gives the idea its weight and inevitability. Substitute another word and the magic collapses.
The Secondary Meaning: To Suspend a Legal Time Limit (Law)

In legal language, "toll" carries a completely separate and unrelated meaning. Here it means to pause, suspend, or temporarily stop the running of a time limit — most commonly a statute of limitations, which is the legal deadline by which a lawsuit must be filed.

For example: "The statute of limitations was tolled while the defendant remained hidden overseas." This means the legal clock was stopped — it did not keep counting — during that period. Once the condition that caused the pause is removed, the clock starts running again.

You will rarely meet this usage outside of legal writing or courtroom contexts. But it is worth knowing it exists, so that if you ever encounter it in a legal document, a news article about a court case, or a crime drama, you are not caught off guard.

If you see the verb toll in a novel, a poem, a film, or everyday speech, it almost certainly means a bell ringing slowly and solemnly — summoning feelings of death, loss, time passing, or grave importance. The image is always the same: something large and heavy, ringing unhurriedly, each stroke landing with full weight before the next one comes.

If you see it in a legal context, it means a clock or deadline has been paused.

Two meanings, very different worlds — but now you know both completely.
16114: A tomahawk is a type of small, light axe that was originally made and used by the Indigenous peoples of North America — the people commonly called Native Americans. Think of it as a cross between a tool and a weapon, small enough to hold and swing with one hand.

A tomahawk has two basic parts:

  • The head — the sharp, heavy part at the top, originally shaped from stone or bone, and later made from iron or steel after Europeans arrived and brought metal. The sharp edge (the blade) is on one side. On the opposite side of the blade, there is often a rounded or flat section called the poll, which can be used for hammering.
  • The handle — a straight wooden stick, usually around 45–60 cm (roughly 18–24 inches) long. It fits through a hole in the head and holds everything together.

Compared to a regular woodcutter's axe, a tomahawk is much lighter and shorter. You can easily carry it at your hip, hold it in one hand, and use it quickly.

Native American tribes across a wide area of North America — from the eastern woodlands to the Great Plains — used the tomahawk. It served multiple purposes in their daily lives:

  1. As a tool: chopping wood, cutting rope, skinning animals, building shelters, and doing other practical camp tasks.
  2. As a weapon in warfare: the tomahawk was effective both in hand-to-hand combat and when thrown at an enemy from a short distance. Because it is light and well-balanced, a skilled person could throw it with great accuracy and force.
  3. As a hunting tool: used to kill or finish off animals.
  4. As a symbol of status or rank: a finely made tomahawk, sometimes decorated with carvings or feathers, could signal that its owner was a warrior or a leader.
The pipe tomahawk — a special kind

One of the most fascinating variations is the pipe tomahawk. This is a tomahawk where the poll (the back of the head, opposite the blade) is shaped into a small pipe bowl, and the handle is hollow, so it works like a smoking pipe. The person could fight with it as a weapon and also smoke tobacco through the same object. These became especially common after European traders and settlers introduced them as trade goods. They held both practical and ceremonial importance.
The tomahawk as a symbol of war and peace

In many Native American traditions, the tomahawk carried deep symbolic meaning beyond its physical use.

  • Taking up the tomahawk meant going to war — deciding to fight.
  • Burying the tomahawk meant making peace — the act of literally placing the weapon in the ground as a sign that fighting was over. This is where the English phrase "bury the hatchet" comes from: it is a simplified version of this Native American peace ceremony. ("Hatchet" is just another word for a small axe.)

This symbolism shows that the tomahawk was not just a physical object — it represented conflict itself, and laying it down represented the end of conflict.

When European settlers arrived in North America, they brought iron and steel with them. Native Americans quickly adopted metal for tomahawk heads because it was stronger, held a sharper edge, and lasted longer than stone. European blacksmiths and traders began making and selling tomahawks specifically for trade with Native tribes. These are called trade tomahawks. Over time, the design merged — it looked similar to a European hatchet but kept the light, balanced form of the traditional Native weapon.

Colonial American soldiers and frontiersmen also started using and carrying tomahawks. It became a recognizable tool of the American frontier life in the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries.

The word and the object both remain very much alive today:

  1. Sport and recreation: Tomahawk throwing is a recognized competitive sport, practiced at festivals, competitions, and clubs around the world. Participants throw tomahawks at wooden targets from set distances, trying to make the blade stick into the wood.
  2. Military use: Modern armed forces — especially US special operations units — still carry tactical tomahawks. These are updated, modern versions made from aircraft-grade steel, and they serve as both a tool (for breaching doors, cutting through obstacles) and a last-resort close-combat weapon.
  3. The Tomahawk missile: The word was famously borrowed to name a type of cruise missile used by the United States military. The BGM-109 Tomahawk is a long-range guided missile that flies low to the ground and can strike targets hundreds of kilometres away. It was named after the weapon because of its speed, precision, and striking power.
  4. Sports culture: The "tomahawk chop" is a hand motion — mimicking the swing of a tomahawk — used by fans of certain sports teams (like the Atlanta Braves in baseball). This practice has been controversial, as many Native Americans consider it a disrespectful caricature of their culture.
  5. In everyday tool use: In countries like Australia and New Zealand, the word "tomahawk" is sometimes used casually to refer to any small, lightweight axe used for camping or outdoor work.
A one-line summary to anchor it all

A tomahawk is a small, one-handed axe of Native American origin, used historically as both a tool and a weapon, symbolic of war and peace, and still present today in sport, military equipment, and popular culture.
16115:
A tome is a large, heavy, thick book — one that is noticeably bigger and weightier than an ordinary book. When you picture a tome, picture something that takes up real space on a shelf, that you might need two hands to carry, and that clearly signals to anyone looking at it: there is a lot of information inside this thing.

But size alone doesn't fully capture what "tome" means. The word also carries a sense of seriousness and depth. A tome isn't just a long book — it's typically a book of significant substance, one that deals with a subject in great detail and thoroughness. Think of a massive history of the Roman Empire, a 900-page medical textbook, a complete encyclopedia of philosophy, or a landmark legal dictionary. These are tomes.
The Three Qualities That Define a Tome

When people use the word "tome," they almost always have three things in mind, working together:

1. Physical size and weight. A tome is visibly and physically large. Its thickness is obvious. It has heft. If someone hands it to you, you feel it.

2. Density of content. A tome is packed with information, analysis, or detail. It is not a light or breezy read. It demands time, attention, and often effort from the reader.

3. Seriousness or authority. A tome tends to be a weighty work in terms of its subject matter too — academic, scholarly, technical, historical, or otherwise important. It gives the impression of being a definitive or comprehensive source on something.

All three qualities tend to travel together. That's what makes "tome" a richer and more specific word than simply saying "a big book."
The Feel and Tone of the Word

"Tome" is a word with a slightly formal, literary, and even old-fashioned feel to it. It has a certain grandeur. When someone uses it, they are subtly suggesting that a book is impressive, significant, or authoritative — even if just in a casual way.

This means it can be used sincerely — with genuine respect for the book's depth and scope — or it can be used with a gentle humor or exaggeration, especially when the speaker wants to tease the idea that something is intimidatingly large. For example, if a friend hands you a 700-page fantasy novel and says, "Here, read this tome," they might be joking about how long it is, or marveling at its size, even if it isn't a scholarly work.

This informal or playful use is perfectly natural and very common in everyday speech. When used this way, it usually still implies size, but the "serious scholarly content" quality is relaxed — the humor comes from applying the grand-sounding word to something more casual.

Here are some sentences to show you how the word is used in practice:

  • "The professor assigned a 600-page tome on the history of the Ottoman Empire." — Used sincerely. A weighty, serious academic book.
  • "I finally finished that massive tome on constitutional law." — Still sincere. A dense, authoritative text.
  • "She pulled a dusty tome off the library shelf and began to read." — Common in storytelling. The image is classic: a grand, old, important book.
  • "My friend gave me this 800-page fantasy tome for my birthday — I'll need a month to get through it." — Informal and slightly humorous. The word "tome" is used for emphasis and mild exaggeration.
  • "He spent three years writing his great tome on Victorian architecture." — Suggests a definitive, thorough, life's-work kind of book.
A Less Common but Valid Use

In certain academic or publishing contexts — particularly in older works, European scholarship, or multi-volume sets — "tome" can specifically refer to one volume within a larger multi-volume work. You might see a series labeled Tome I, Tome II, Tome III, much like how a long encyclopedia might be split across several books. In this technical sense, "tome" just means one book of a larger set, regardless of whether that single volume is very thick. However, this usage is relatively rare in modern everyday English, and if you encounter it, it will almost always be clearly labeled. In everyday conversation, the first meaning — a large, weighty, serious book — is the one you need.

If you want to anchor the word to a single, clear image: think of the biggest, heaviest, most densely packed book you have ever seen — the kind that sits on a scholar's desk, looks like it took decades to write, and holds a lifetime of knowledge within it. That is a tome. The word is a compliment to the book's scope and seriousness, and sometimes, a gentle laugh at just how much reading lies ahead.
16116:
Tomfoolery means silly, foolish, or playful behavior — the kind that is goofy, ridiculous, or lacking in seriousness. It describes what someone does when they are clowning around, messing about, or acting in a way that has no real purpose other than being absurd or mischievous.

Think of it this way: if someone is making strange faces, playing a pointless prank, goofing off when they should be working, or doing something comically stupid — that is tomfoolery.

Tomfoolery covers a wide range of silly actions. Here are some clear examples of what qualifies:

  • Two students throwing paper balls at each other during a serious class.
  • An adult making ridiculous sounds to entertain themselves at an inappropriate time.
  • A group of friends daring each other to do something pointless and absurd.
  • Someone pretending to fall down dramatically just to get a laugh.
  • Pulling a harmless but silly prank on a coworker.

The key idea is that the behavior is not serious, not productive, and often a little ridiculous — but it is also not deeply criminal or evil. It sits in the zone of "this is dumb and possibly annoying, but it's not the end of the world."
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

This is where tomfoolery gets interesting. The word carries a mild disapproval mixed with a hint of amusement. When someone uses this word, they are not furious or deeply offended — they are more like exasperated or eye-rolling, sometimes even secretly amused.

Think of a strict but fair grandparent watching children act silly at the dinner table and saying, "Enough of this tomfoolery!" They are scolding, yes — but not in a frightening way. There is a lightness to the word.

This means the word itself has a slightly old-fashioned, warm, and even humorous quality. Using "tomfoolery" can make you sound playful yourself, even while you are criticizing silly behavior. It is not a cold, clinical word. It has personality.

Tomfoolery almost always refers to behavior that is mostly harmless, or at least not seriously dangerous. If someone robs a bank, you would not call that "tomfoolery." If someone sticks a "kick me" note on a friend's back, that is tomfoolery.

However, tomfoolery can sometimes edge into being disruptive or annoying — wasting people's time, interrupting important things, or making it hard to get anything done. So while it is not evil, it is not always purely innocent either. It can be mildly problematic.

As a noun, tomfoolery is usually uncountable — meaning you typically do not say "a tomfoolery" or "two tomfooleries." You simply say:

  • "There was a lot of tomfoolery going on."
  • "I'm tired of all this tomfoolery."
  • "Stop the tomfoolery!"

However, in rare or literary use, the plural form tomfooleries does exist and refers to specific individual acts of foolishness:

  • "The tomfooleries of his youth are well-documented."

In everyday speech, the singular uncountable form is by far the most common.

Here are the most natural ways you will see and use this word:

  • "Stop this/the tomfoolery." → Telling someone to stop acting silly.
  • "I have no time for such tomfoolery." → Dismissing silly behavior as a waste of time.
  • "There's always some tomfoolery going on." → Describing an environment where people goof off regularly.
  • "Enough tomfoolery — let's get serious." → Transitioning from play to seriousness.
  • "His tomfoolery got him into trouble." → When silly behavior has real consequences.

Knowing the similar words helps you understand tomfoolery's exact position in the language.

  • Silliness — almost identical, but slightly softer and more innocent.
  • Nonsense — broader; can mean silly talk or ideas, not just behavior.
  • Shenanigans — very close; slightly more mischievous, implying trickery or sneakiness.
  • Horseplay — specifically physical rough-and-tumble foolishness.
  • Buffoonery — similar, but emphasizes acting like a clown; slightly more theatrical.
  • Antics — refers to specific funny or wild acts, often used affectionately.
  • Clowning around — informal phrase, same idea, but more casual.

Tomfoolery sits comfortably among all of these, but it has its own distinct flavor: it is slightly more old-fashioned, slightly more broad (covering behavior in general, not just physical or sneaky acts), and carries that particular blend of mild annoyance and amusement.

To sharpen your understanding, here is what the word does not mean:

  • It is not serious wrongdoing (crime, cruelty, genuine harm).
  • It is not stupidity in thinking (you wouldn't call a flawed argument "tomfoolery").
  • It is not a compliment (even when said with a smile, it gently criticizes the behavior).
  • It is not passive — it always refers to active behavior, things someone is doing, not just a state of being.

If you had to lock the meaning into one sentence, it would be this:

Tomfoolery is silly, playful, and pointless behavior that lacks seriousness — harmless enough to smile at, but foolish enough to warrant a mild scolding.

It is the word you reach for when someone is goofing off, acting ridiculous, or making a situation less serious than it should be — and you want to call it out with a word that is firm but not harsh, disapproving but not angry, and just a little bit charming in itself.
16117: The word toner refers to a substance — usually a fine powder, liquid, or chemical — that is used to add, change, or fix color or tone onto a surface. It appears in several different fields, each with a distinct meaning.

This is the most common use of the word.

When you print a document using a laser printer or make a copy on a photocopier, the machine doesn't use liquid ink the way a pen does. Instead, it uses toner — an extremely fine, dry powder made mostly of tiny plastic and carbon particles, sometimes mixed with pigment for color.

Here's how it works in simple terms: The printer uses static electricity to attract the toner powder onto the paper in the exact shape of your text or image. Then, a heated roller melts and fuses the powder permanently onto the paper. That's why a freshly printed laser page feels warm and the print never smudges the way wet ink might.

Toner comes in a small cartridge that you slot into the printer. When it runs out, you replace the cartridge. A single toner cartridge can print thousands of pages because the powder is used very sparingly.

Key idea: Toner in printing is a dry powder that gets melted onto paper — not sprayed like ink.

In skincare, a toner is a lightweight, water-based liquid that you apply to your face — typically right after washing it and before applying moisturizer.

Its main jobs are:

  • Removing leftover residue — after washing your face, there can still be traces of makeup, oil, or cleanser. Toner helps wipe those away.
  • Balancing the skin's pH — your skin has a natural slightly acidic state that keeps it healthy. Washing can disrupt this. Toner helps restore that balance.
  • Preparing skin — it preps your skin to absorb the next products (like serums or moisturizers) more effectively.
  • Hydrating or treating — many modern toners also contain ingredients that hydrate the skin or address specific concerns like acne, dullness, or dryness.

You apply it by pouring a little onto a cotton pad and gently sweeping it across your face, or sometimes patting it directly with your hands.

Older toners (especially from decades past) were often harsh and alcohol-heavy — they would strip the skin. Modern toners are much gentler and are often marketed as "hydrating toners," "exfoliating toners" (containing mild acids that remove dead skin cells), or "brightening toners."

Key idea: A skincare toner is a liquid that refreshes, balances, and prepares your skin — used as a step in your daily face-care routine.

In hair care, a toner is a product — usually a liquid, gloss, or dye-like formula — used to adjust or neutralize the color of hair, especially after bleaching.

When hair is bleached (lightened), it often turns yellow or orange before reaching a pale blonde or white color. This unwanted warmth is something many people want to eliminate. A toner deposits a cool or neutral color (usually ash, violet, or beige tones) onto the hair to cancel out the brassiness, leaving the hair looking platinum, silver, icy blonde, or a more refined shade.

Think of it like color theory: if your hair has too much yellow, you apply a purple-toned toner, because purple cancels yellow. If it has too much orange, you apply a blue-toned toner.

Hair toners are also used to:

  • Fine-tune a hair color after dyeing (e.g., making a brown look cooler or warmer)
  • Add a subtle tint (like rose gold or smoky gray) without a full dye job
  • Refresh faded color between salon visits

Toners in hair care are typically temporary to semi-permanent — they wash out over several weeks, unlike permanent hair dye.

Key idea: A hair toner neutralizes unwanted warm or off tones in bleached or colored hair, refining it into a cleaner, more desired shade.

In traditional film-based (darkroom) photography, a toner is a chemical solution used to alter the color of a developed black-and-white photograph.

A standard black-and-white photo has gray and black tones. By soaking the print in a toner chemical, photographers can shift those tones to warmer or cooler hues:

  • Sepia toner gives photos a warm, brownish color — the classic "old photograph" look.
  • Blue toner gives a cool, blue-tinted appearance.
  • Gold toner can add subtle warmth and also increases the longevity of a print.

Beyond just aesthetics, toners can also chemically stabilize a photograph, making it more resistant to fading over time.

This use of the word is less common in everyday conversation today, since digital photography has largely replaced film, but it's still relevant in fine art and traditional photography communities.

Key idea: In darkroom photography, a toner is a chemical bath that changes the color tone of a black-and-white photo for artistic or preservation purposes.

The thread connecting all these meanings is the core idea of the word tone — which refers to a shade, hue, or quality of color. A toner, in every context, is something that adjusts, fixes, or adds tone:

  • In printing, it creates the tones (the dark and light areas) of a printed image.
  • In skincare, it restores and balances the skin's natural tone and condition.
  • In hair care, it corrects and refines the color tone of your hair.
  • In photography, it changes the color tone of a photo for artistic effect.

The exact form toner takes — powder, liquid, cream, or chemical — depends entirely on the field, but its role is always about controlling or influencing tone.
16118:
Tongs are a tool made of two arms joined together, used to grip, pick up, hold, or move objects — especially when you cannot or should not use your bare hands.

Think of it this way: your hand has fingers that open and close to grab things. Tongs work in almost the same way, but they are made of metal (or sometimes plastic), they are much longer than your fingers, and they act as an extension of your hand.

Tongs have a very simple structure:

  • Two long arms (also called legs or jaws), placed side by side.
  • The arms are connected at one end — this is where you hold them. The connection is either a hinge (like a pivot point) or a simple bend or spring in the material.
  • The other end is the gripping end — the part that actually touches and holds the object. This end can be flat, curved, ridged, or shaped differently depending on what the tongs are designed for.

If you look at a basic pair of kitchen tongs, it looks almost like a long, narrow U shape or like a very wide, stretched-out pair of scissors.

The mechanism is beautifully simple:

  • When you squeeze the two arms together at the handle end, the gripping end either opens or closes, depending on the design.
  • Spring-loaded tongs (like kitchen or salad tongs) stay naturally open. You squeeze the handles to close the gripping end around an object, and when you let go, the tongs spring back open.
  • Pivot-style tongs (like blacksmith tongs or fireplace tongs) work more like scissors or pliers — the arms cross over a central pivot point, so squeezing the handles closes the gripping end.

In both cases, the result is the same: you can grab something, hold onto it, and move it without touching it with your fingers.

Tongs solve several problems at once:

  • Heat protection. You can pick up something extremely hot (a piece of meat on a grill, a hot coal in a fireplace, a red-hot piece of metal in a forge) without burning your hands.
  • Hygiene. In food service, cooks and servers use tongs to handle food without touching it with bare hands.
  • Reach. Tongs let you reach into deep pots, tight spaces, or dangerous areas where putting your hand would be risky.
  • Grip on awkward objects. Some things are slippery, oddly shaped, or too large to hold with fingers alone — tongs give you a secure grip on them.

Tongs appear in many areas of life, and their shape is always adapted to their specific job:

In the kitchen:

  • Cooking tongs / kitchen tongs — the most common type. Used for turning meat, tossing pasta, flipping vegetables, or serving food. Usually made of stainless steel with a spring mechanism.
  • Salad tongs — used for tossing and serving salads. Often come as a matched pair of a spoon and a fork joined at the handle end.
  • Ice tongs — small tongs used to pick up individual ice cubes. The gripping ends are often curved or clawed to hold the slippery cube firmly.
  • Sugar tongs — tiny, delicate tongs shaped like a small claw or a pair of mini arms, used to pick up individual sugar cubes and place them in tea or coffee.

At the fireplace or grill:

  • Fireplace tongs — long, heavy tongs used to move burning logs or coal in a fireplace safely.
  • Barbecue tongs / grill tongs — longer than kitchen tongs, so your hands stay far from the heat of the grill while you flip or move food.

In industry and craft:

  • Blacksmith tongs (or forge tongs) — heavy-duty, pivot-style tongs used by blacksmiths to hold pieces of extremely hot metal while shaping them on an anvil. They come in many shapes depending on the shape of metal being held.

In science and medicine:

  • Laboratory tongs — used to hold hot test tubes, beakers, or crucibles in a chemistry lab.
  • Medical forceps — a closely related tool used by doctors to grip tissue or objects during procedures. (These are sometimes called tongs in casual speech, though "forceps" is the precise medical term.)

"Tongs" is almost always used in the plural form. You do not normally say "a tong" — you say "tongs" or "a pair of tongs."

This is similar to other tools and clothing items in English that always appear in the plural: scissors, pants, glasses, pliers. Even though you are talking about one single tool, you use the plural word.

✅ "Hand me the tongs, please."
✅ "I need a pair of tongs to flip this steak."
❌ "Hand me the tong." (This sounds unnatural and wrong in almost all contexts.)

When counting them, you use the phrase "a pair of tongs" for one tool, and "two pairs of tongs" for two tools.
A Simple Way to Remember It

Tongs = two arms that work together to grip something your hand cannot or should not touch.

Whether it's a sizzling piece of chicken on a grill, a burning log in a fireplace, a delicate sugar cube, or a glowing-hot piece of metal in a forge — tongs are always there to do the gripping safely, cleanly, and precisely.
16119: The word tonic has several distinct meanings depending on the context — medicine, music, drinks, and everyday speech. The good news is that a single core idea quietly connects most of them: the idea of something that restores, strengthens, or brings a sense of balance and wholeness. Keep that in mind as you read through each meaning.

This is the oldest and most traditional meaning. A tonic is any drink, syrup, or medicine that is meant to make you feel stronger, healthier, or more energetic — especially after a period of weakness or illness.

Think of it as a "pick-me-up." Before modern medicine, people took tonics made from herbs, roots, and minerals to boost their general health. Even today, you'll find products sold as "hair tonics," "liver tonics," or "herbal tonics" in pharmacies and health shops.

Examples in a sentence:

  • "The doctor recommended an iron tonic to help with her fatigue."
  • "My grandmother swore by her daily tonic of apple cider vinegar and honey."

The key idea: a tonic doesn't just cure one specific disease — it generally strengthens and revitalizes the body as a whole.

You've almost certainly seen or heard of this one. Tonic water is a fizzy, carbonated soft drink with a slightly bitter taste. That bitterness comes from an ingredient called quinine, which was originally used as a medicine to treat malaria. Over time, people began mixing it with water and sugar to make it easier to drink — and tonic water was born.

In everyday conversation, people often just call it "a tonic" for short. It's very commonly used as a mixer in cocktails. The most famous example is the gin and tonic, where gin is mixed with tonic water.

Examples in a sentence:

  • "Could I have a gin and tonic, please?"
  • "She doesn't drink alcohol, so she ordered a tonic water with lime."

Plain tonic water is not the same as sparkling water — it has that distinct bitter, slightly sweet flavour that comes from the quinine. If you've never tried it, imagine a very lightly sweetened lemonade, but with a dry, bitter finish instead of sourness.
3. Something That Lifts Your Spirits (Figurative Use)

This is a beautiful, everyday use of the word. In informal and literary English, you can call anything a "tonic" if it makes you feel refreshed, happier, or more alive — even if it has nothing to do with medicine or drinks.

Think of it this way: just as a health tonic revives your body, a "tonic" in this figurative sense revives your mood, spirit, or energy.

Examples in a sentence:

  • "After a difficult week at work, the long walk in the countryside was a real tonic."
  • "Her sense of humour was a tonic to everyone in the room."
  • "Fresh air and sunshine are the best tonic I know."

This is a very natural and common usage in British English especially. When someone says something was "a tonic," they mean it genuinely refreshed them or lifted them up.
4. In Music: The First Note of a Scale

In music theory, the tonic refers to the first note of a musical scale, and it is arguably the single most important note in any piece of music.

Here's the idea simply explained:

When music is written in a particular key — say, the key of C major — all the notes in that piece revolve around one central note: the note C. That central, "home base" note is called the tonic.

The tonic is the note that feels like rest, resolution, and arrival. When a melody wanders away from it and eventually comes back to it, you feel a satisfying sense of "we're home." It's why the last note of a song, when it lands on the tonic, feels so complete and settled.

A simple analogy: Imagine you go on a long journey, visit many different places, and then finally come home. Your home is the tonic. No matter how far the music travels, the tonic is always where it belongs.

Examples in a sentence:

  • "In the key of G major, the note G is the tonic."
  • "The melody kept moving away from the tonic, creating tension, before finally resolving back to it at the end."

If you've ever felt that satisfying "completion" feeling when a song ends, you've felt the power of the tonic.

In beauty and skincare, a tonic (also called a skin tonic or hair tonic) is a liquid product that you apply to your skin or scalp to cleanse, refresh, or condition it.

A skin tonic is used after washing your face — it removes any leftover dirt or cleanser, tightens the pores, and prepares your skin for moisturizer. It's similar to a toner, though the two words are sometimes used interchangeably.

A hair tonic is rubbed into the scalp to promote healthy hair, reduce dryness, or simply to keep hair looking neat and groomed.

Examples in a sentence:

  • "He smoothed a little hair tonic through his hair before combing it."
  • "Apply the skin tonic with a cotton pad after cleansing."

Here's a quick way to remember all the meanings:

ContextWhat "tonic" means
Health/medicineA strengthening drink or remedy
DrinksBitter fizzy water, used in cocktails
Everyday speechAnything that refreshes or cheers you up
MusicThe "home base" note of a key
Skincare/haircareA liquid lotion for skin or hair

In health, a tonic strengthens you. In a glass, it's the bitter fizzy water you mix with gin. In everyday life, anything that lifts your mood can be called a tonic. In music, it's the home note that everything resolves to. And in a bathroom cabinet, it's a lotion for your skin or hair.

The thread running through nearly all of these is the same: a tonic brings you back to a state of strength, balance, or wholeness — whether that's your body, your mood, or a musical phrase finding its way home.
